explanations.explanation: I see why you'd say that, friend, because Mark does say Jesus didn't want anyone to know He was there. But the same verse says He "…was unable to escape their notice." (Mark 7:24) So the visit did not stay a secret. That's like a surprise party the whole office already knows about.

That's right, friend. Mark says Jesus entered the house not wanting anyone to know He was there, but He "…was unable to escape their notice." (Mark 7:24) Word got around anyway. A house with a secret in it is a lot like a bakery with a fresh batch in it, because somebody always finds out.
Right, friend. Mark says she heard about Jesus, "…and she came and fell at His feet." (Mark 7:25) She ended up right at His feet. I think that tells you how much her little girl mattered to her.
Mark doesn't mention a door, friend. He says she heard about Jesus, "…and she came and fell at His feet." (Mark 7:25) The text puts her at His feet. Waiting outside isn't part of what Mark tells us.

explanations.answer: She sends word to His disciples
explanations.explanation: Sending a message sounds sensible, friend, but the text doesn't say she did. Mark says she heard about Jesus, "…and she came and fell at His feet." (Mark 7:25) She went herself. Mark doesn't mention anyone passing messages for her.

Close, friend, but Mark puts it differently. He says she "…kept asking Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter." (Mark 7:26) Kept asking means she asked again and again, not once. I think that's a mom who wasn't leaving without an answer.

That's it, friend. Mark says she "…kept asking Jesus to drive the demon out of her daughter." (Mark 7:26) That's not one polite question and a wave goodbye. She kept on asking, and I think that's one stubborn kind of love.

explanations.answer: Even the dogs under the table eat the crumbs
explanations.explanation: That's what she says, friend. She answers, "Yes, Lord," and then adds, "even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs." (Mark 7:28) She takes what Jesus said and answers right inside it. I can't answer anybody that well even when I get three days to think.

explanations.answer: The children are already full of bread
explanations.explanation: That's not her answer, friend. Jesus says to let the children have their fill first (Mark 7:27), and she doesn't argue with that. She says, "Yes, Lord," and then, "even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs." (Mark 7:28)

explanations.answer: The dogs can wait until the next meal
explanations.explanation: She doesn't say anything about waiting, friend. Her words are "Yes, Lord," and then "even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs." (Mark 7:28) Her point is about the crumbs under the table. Nobody in her answer is put off until later.

explanations.answer: The demon has left your daughter
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus says, "Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter." (Mark 7:29) He says it as already done. Mark tells us the woman went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone (Mark 7:30).

explanations.answer: Bring your daughter here to Me
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask for that, friend. He tells her, "…you may go. The demon has left your daughter." (Mark 7:29) The girl never has to be brought to Him. Mark says the mom went home and found her child there (Mark 7:30).

explanations.answer: Your daughter will be well tomorrow
explanations.explanation: No waiting until tomorrow, friend. Jesus says, "The demon has left your daughter." (Mark 7:29) That's past tense, so it had already happened. Mark never mentions a tomorrow in this story.

That's right, friend. Mark says the woman "…went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone." (Mark 7:30) What Jesus told her was exactly what she found. I think that's one very good homecoming.

It's true, friend. Mark says she "…went home and found her child lying on the bed, and the demon was gone." (Mark 7:30) She came home to the very thing Jesus had told her. I think she walked in that door with a lot on her heart.

Yes, friend. Mark says the people "…begged Jesus to place His hand on him." (Mark 7:32) They brought the man to Jesus and begged for exactly that. I think bringing someone to Jesus like that shows how much they cared about him.

explanations.answer: Pray for him at the synagogue
explanations.explanation: Mark doesn't mention a synagogue here, friend. He says the people brought the man to Jesus, "…and they begged Jesus to place His hand on him." (Mark 7:32) The ask was about Jesus' hand. The place doesn't come up.
No priests in this scene, friend. Mark says the people "…begged Jesus to place His hand on him." (Mark 7:32) They brought the man straight to Jesus. They asked Him for something, not for directions.

I get why you'd think so, friend, with all those people around. But Mark says Jesus "…took him aside privately, away from the crowd…" (Mark 7:33) So the healing happened away from the crowd, not in the middle of it.
That's right, friend. Mark says Jesus "…took him aside privately, away from the crowd…" (Mark 7:33) The crowd stayed back. I think a quiet spot has its own kind of kindness.

Yes, friend. Mark says Jesus "…put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue." (Mark 7:33) The man was deaf and hardly able to speak, and those are the two places Jesus touched. Those touches matched the two troubles the man had.

Not those two, friend. Mark says Jesus "…put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue." (Mark 7:33) That's the ears and the tongue. Eyes don't come up in this scene, and the hand comes up only in the people's request (Mark 7:32).

That's not it, friend. Mark says Jesus "…put His fingers into the man’s ears. Then He spit and touched the man’s tongue." (Mark 7:33) So the touches were on his ears and his tongue. Head and chest aren't mentioned.

That's the word, friend. Jesus says, "Ephphatha!" and Mark adds, "(which means, 'Be opened!')" (Mark 7:34) One word and nothing else. Right after, Mark says the man's ears were opened and his tongue was released (Mark 7:35).

Good try, friend, but that's not the word here. Mark says Jesus said, "Ephphatha!" and explains, "(which means, 'Be opened!')" (Mark 7:34) Nothing in this scene is being told to be still. Something is being told to open.

Not strong, friend. Mark tells us "Ephphatha!" means "Be opened!" (Mark 7:34) Opened fits what happened next, when Mark says the man's ears were opened and his tongue was released (Mark 7:35). Strength never comes up in this verse.

That's right, friend. Mark says, "Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly." (Mark 7:35) He didn't have to wait around or practice. He went from deaf to hearing and speaking plainly.

It's true, friend. Mark says, "Immediately the man’s ears were opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly." (Mark 7:35) There wasn't a wait or a slow recovery. It happened right then.

explanations.answer: The more He orders them the more they tell it
explanations.explanation: That's what Mark says, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) The harder Jesus pushed for quiet, the louder the news got. That's how good news goes.

explanations.answer: They keep it to themselves for a while
explanations.explanation: Mark doesn't say that, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) The more Jesus ordered, the more widely they proclaimed it. Keeping it to themselves isn't what Mark describes.

explanations.answer: They tell only their own families
explanations.explanation: Mark never says they told only their families, friend. "But the more He ordered them, the more widely they proclaimed it." (Mark 7:36) Mark's word is widely, and he mentions no small circle. The news traveled.
That's the first blank, friend. The people say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) Hear is exactly what the deaf man got to do. His ears were opened (Mark 7:35).

That's the second blank, friend. The people say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) The man's tongue was released, and he began to speak plainly (Mark 7:35). The people's astonishment came out in those words.

That's a good word, friend, but it isn't what the people say here. They say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) This man's trouble was with ears and speech. Seeing isn't part of this scene.

Walking isn't in this crowd's words, friend. They say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) That matches the man whose ears were opened and whose tongue was released (Mark 7:35). His ears and his tongue were the story.

It's a nice word, friend, but it's not what they say. The people say, "He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!" (Mark 7:37) Mark says they were utterly astonished. Their words are about ears and speech.
